newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters agree to end strike. [CORRECTED 10:32 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters agree to end strike. [CORRECTED 10:32 GMT]

text.p: The Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service have agreed to end a bitter 15-day strike, the biggest U.S. labor walkout in two decades, Labor Secretary Alexis Herman announced early on Tuesday.

Union President Ron Carey declared victory and said the Teamsters won sweeping concessions for additional full-time jobs, better union pensions and improved pay that "sends a signal that American workers are on the move again."
The company, which had insisted its July 30th proposal was its "last, best and final" offer, had no immediate comment. Earlier, it said the strike had cost it $650 million.
Carey said the 185,000 strikers, who subsisted on $55-a-week strike benefits, may return to work as soon as Wednesday.

The agreement was also a major victory for Herman. The labor secretary brought the parties back to the bargaining table on Thursday for marathon talks. Negotiations lasted nearly 90 hours, with scant time off for sleep, until a deal was hammered out.

"I am pleased to announce that the United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union have reached a tentative settlement," declared the labor secretary, flanked by negotiators for both sides and the federal negotiators who guided them.
Carey held his own news conference at union headquarters a few minutes later.

"In virtually every area this agreement is much, much better than the last offer before the strike," Carey said, ticking off the details. In UPS's headquarters city of Atlanta, thousands of striking Teamsters cheered the announcement.

But the company had warned workers it would lay off 15,000 when they returned because the strike had damaged its long-term business. Carey conceded that the company would have to carry out at least some temporary layoffs.

The union won on its key issue, the conversion of part-time jobs to full-time. The union demanded and won the conversion of 10,000 jobs over the five-year life of the contract, while the company originally offered only 1,000, Carey said. (Corrects the number of jobs to be converted, from 20,000 to 10,000, and also corrects the number of jobs UPS originally offered to convert, from 11,000 to 1,000.)

Carey said the union turned back the company's demand to pull out of the Teamsters multi-employer pension plans and start a new company-controlled pension plan and won generous new benefits. He said a retiring 30-year worker would get monthly benefits of $3,000 or more.
The agreement will phase out over six months the use of subcontractors, except during the crush of holiday package shipping, giving the jobs instead to UPS workers, he said.

Full-time workers gain $3.10 over five years, while part-timers gain $4.10 over the same period, he said. Top-rate full-time employees will receive $23 hourly, while top-rate part-timers will move up to about $15 from $11, he said.
And Carey said if the company wants to raise the package weight limit again it must negotiate again with the union.
Carey aimed his remarks at a broader audience of Americans who had backed the Teamsters strike in public opinion polls.
He said employers have cut jobs, pensions, health coverage and "stepped on workers' rights" since President Ronald Reagan fired striking air traffic controllers in 1981.

"Working people were on the run, but not anymore," he declared. "This strike marks a new era. American workers have shown that if we stand up to corporate greed, this victory sends a signal that American workers are on the move again.
"Working families are telling big companies that we will fight for the American dream," he said.
President Bill Clinton patted both sides on the back in an early-morning statement read to reporters in Edgartown, Massachusetts, where he was on vacation.
"Today's agreement represents their hard work and determination to reconcile their differences for the good of the company, its employees and the customers they serve," Clinton said.
"The issues that were at the heart of their negotiations are important to our nation's economic strength, and to all Americans."
Before the strike began UPS handled 12 million items on a normal weekday. It now has 8 million packages in its system and accepted no new packages for ground delivery during the strike.
The chief UPS negotiator, Dave Murray, joined Carey in paying tribute to Herman, the labor secretary, for having nursed the contract talks to a successful conclusion.
Murray said the company wanted to address its employees before speaking publicly.
The strike was the largest in the United States since a three-day Teamsters freight strike of 400,000 truckers in 1976.
